answer.label: Not Terry Pratchett — an old proverb he quoted
answer.authorDates: Folk saying · roots in Jonathan Swift, 1710 · boots version in print by 1820
answer.sourceLine: Pratchett did put these exact words in his Discworld novel The Truth (2000), but his characters present them as a saying that already existed (“Apparently, they say…”). Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying back to Jonathan Swift in 1710. It finds the boots form in 1820 and shows Charles Haddon Spurgeon calling it “the old Proverb” in 1855.

source.heading: Where Pratchett used it

docMeta.dd: Spoken by characters as an existing saying, not as Pratchett’s coinage
Swift, 1710; boots form by 1820; Spurgeon’s “old Proverb,” 1855

source.excerpt: …saying, sir, that a lie can run round the world before the truth has got its boots on.’ ‘Ha! Did you just make that up…
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying from Swift (1710) through the 1820 “pulling her boots on” form and Spurgeon’s 1855 “old Proverb.” It notes that Pratchett used the saying “several times” in The Truth (2000), and it finds no substantive support for crediting Twain or Churchill.
An Internet Archive full-text search ↗ finds the exact wording “a lie can run round the world before the truth has got its boots on” in the 2000 Doubleday and HarperCollins editions of The Truth.

The Annotated Pratchett File ↗ lists a third use in the novel (“lies could run round the world before the truth could get its boots on”) and glosses it as an existing saying that has been attributed to others.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the near-identical “halfway round the world before the truth has got its boots on” as misattributed to James Callaghan, calling it a very old paraphrase that was in print in that form by 1939.
source.excerptNote: This text comes from Internet Archive full-text snippets of the 2000 editions of The Truth; the ellipses mark where a snippet starts or stops. Elsewhere in the novel, Mr. Slant says the phrase again with a disclaimer: “Apparently, they say, a lie can run around the world before the truth has got its boots on. What an obnoxious little phrase, don’t you think?” That line is quoted from the US paperback, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗.

author.name: Anonymous proverb
author.heading: Where the saying comes from
author.metaLine: Folk saying · roots in Jonathan Swift, 1710 · boots version in print by 1820
author.bio: This saying has no single author. Quote Investigator traces a whole family of sayings about fast lies and slow truth back to Jonathan Swift’s 1710 line “Falsehood flies, and the Truth comes limping after it.” The truth-pulling-on-its-boots image was in print by 1820. In an 1855 sermon, Charles Haddon Spurgeon quoted it as “the old Proverb.” Over time the wording has drifted from boots to shoes, breeches and pants.

misattribution.heading: Who gets credited, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: The saying about a lie racing ahead of the truth has been pinned on many famous names. None of them coined it.

items.why: He did write the line in The Truth (2000), but his characters frame it as an existing saying (“Apparently, they say…”, “Did you just make that up”). Quote Investigator ↗ lists his use as one late entry in a long chain of versions.

items.scope: “halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes”
items.why: Twain died in 1910, and the earliest credit to him that Quote Investigator ↗ found is from 1919, which QI judges not substantive. A 1987 Twain collection prints the “shoes” version only as “Attributed.”

items.scope: “before the truth has a chance to get its pants on”
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ calls a 1981 attribution to Churchill implausible, and notes that Churchill expert Richard M. Langworth listed the saying among lines Churchill never said.

items.scope: “halfway round the world before the truth has got its boots on”
items.why: The line is widely quoted from a Commons speech of his, but Wikiquote ↗ lists it as misattributed: an old paraphrase that was in print in that form by 1939.

items.who: Thomas Jefferson, Fisher Ames, John Randolph
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ shows the saying was already credited to each of them in the 1820s–1840s. It calls the Jefferson attribution implausible, and an 1846 review called the saying a Chinese proverb.

misattribution.truthLine: This is an anonymous proverb, and its wording has been changing for more than three hundred years, as Quote Investigator ↗ puts it. Swift can be credited with his own 1710 line, Spurgeon popularized a boots version in 1855, and Pratchett used it in 2000. None of them invented the boots saying.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Pratchett
lead: Pratchett never claimed the line. In The Truth, a novel about lies, rumor and the press, the saying keeps coming back. Each time, a character treats it as received wisdom. One asks whether another “just made that up,” and Mr. Slant, who says he has “spent centuries in courtrooms,” calls it “an obnoxious little phrase.”

Lifted out of the novel, the sentence lost that framing and started circulating as a Pratchett original. Quote collections helped. The Internet Archive’s full-text index shows Seriously Funny (London: Doubleday, 2016), a book of Pratchett quotations, printing the line under The Truth.
context.pull: “Apparently, they say, a lie can run around the world before the truth has got its boots on.”
